stories.title: MOX names Justin Melnikoff Chief Operating Officer
stories.summary: The fibre network operator is stepping up expansion plans to meet surging demand from cloud and AI customers across subsea and land routes.
stories.title_zh: MOX任命Justin Melnikoff为首席运营官
stories.content:
MOX Networks has appointed Justin Melnikoff as Chief Operating Officer, returning a former executive to the leadership team.

Melnikoff previously held the role before moving into a non-operating position as Strategic Advisor and Board Member. He will now work with Chief Executive Officer Allen Meeks on network expansion, business development and strategic partnerships as the fibre network operator expands its infrastructure footprint.

The appointment comes as MOX builds out both terrestrial and subsea assets. Recent investments include fibre pairs on Google's Topaz subsea cable, which links North America and Japan, and Google's Firmina subsea cable, which connects North America and Brazil.

MOX is also preparing multiple terrestrial network expansions in 2027 as part of a strategy to serve demand from data centre hubs, cloud providers, hyperscalers and artificial intelligence infrastructure.

### Executive return

Melnikoff returns to an executive role after serving in advisory and board positions. MOX said he brings more than 20 years of experience in digital infrastructure, including strategic alliances, acquisitions and divestitures, commercial negotiations and infrastructure development.

His previous roles include senior leadership positions at MOX and Agile Networks, as well as corporate development work at Sidera Networks. He has also advised firms investing in digital infrastructure.

The appointment brings back a familiar figure as network operators expand routes and capacity to meet rising traffic from cloud computing and AI workloads. Subsea and long-haul terrestrial links have attracted growing investment as operators seek direct connections between major markets and data centre clusters.

MOX describes itself as a fibre-optic network specialist operating across terrestrial and subsea networks. Its business includes linking major data centre hubs and providing connectivity for customers with large bandwidth requirements.

Meeks said Melnikoff had been closely involved with the business for a long time.

"Justin has played an instrumental role throughout MOX's existence and I'm thrilled to have him back in an executive leadership capacity," said Allen Meeks, Chief Executive Officer, MOX Networks.

"He brings an invaluable combination of industry knowledge, commercial experience, and strategic reasoning to the business. As we focus on expanding our infrastructure portfolio and pursuing new opportunities, having Justin working alongside me and our leadership team day in and day out puts us in an even stronger position to execute and deliver for our customers," Meeks said.

### Expansion focus

Recent subsea investments reflect a broader push by infrastructure groups into routes linking North America with key international markets. The Topaz system provides a Pacific link to Japan, while Firmina extends connectivity to Brazil, giving MOX access to two strategically important corridors for international traffic.

Those moves sit alongside planned terrestrial builds that would extend the company's reach on land as demand rises for resilient, lower-latency routes between network nodes. Operators across the sector have been expanding in response to traffic growth from AI model training, cloud services and data-heavy enterprise applications.

Melnikoff said those changes in traffic patterns were central to his return.

"I'm excited to come back to an organization that is stronger than ever before and with endless opportunities ahead of us," said Justin Melnikoff, Chief Operating Officer, MOX Networks.

"As AI and other data-intensive applications reshape network requirements, our focus is on ensuring we have the infrastructure, partnerships, and commercial capabilities to support what comes next. I'm excited to once again work with the team to take MOX to the next level," Melnikoff said.

stories.content:
It has sold US$2.4 billion worth of licensed products to the Asian country in Q3

\[WASHINGTON\] Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre chips to China, despite winning the US government’s blessing to sell a version of that model to the Asian nation in 2025.

The world’s leading AI chip supplier sold US$2.4 billion worth of licensed, Hopper data centre products to China in the third quarter, Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive officer, said during an earnings call with analysts on Tuesday (Nov 17).

But the company’s future “guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data centre products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data centre products to China”, she said.

Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments were ending.

Still, the confirmation is a notable shift in stance for a company that has spent years fighting for the right to do more business with Chinese customers.

Jensen Huang, who was ousted as CEO of Nvidia last week following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, had been the loudest advocate for exports to China.

Huang departed after disclosing an affair with a woman who is now under investigation by the US government for potentially aiding China’s spy agency and possibly helping smuggle chips to China.

Beijing has denied that it attempted to spy on Huang.

On Monday, the Trump administration moved to apply more scrutiny to exports of processors to several countries and limit any chip sales abroad when the data centre buying them plans to provide Chinese companies remote access to advanced AI chips and servers.

At one point, Nvidia had pushed the US government for permission sell advanced Blackwell chips to China.

The Trump administration never acquiesced to that request, but US President Donald Trump blessed the sale of the Hopper processors known as H200s, which are two generations behind Nvidia’s leading Rubin family of chips, highlighting the strong personal relationship that Huang had built with Trump.

Harvey Jones, who was appointed Nvidia’s first chair last week, said the company’s board recognises that it’s “living in a world” where “national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace”.

The company’s next CEO will need to “navigate those waters very carefully”, he said.

Nvidia has also announced that it was forming a board committee dedicated to national security and export controls.

The company on Tuesday boosted its sales forecast for 2027 and vowed to improve Nvidia’s access to critical supplies, while tamping down speculation that Huang might return. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Climate risk reshapes Asia Pacific data centre plans
stories.summary: More than two-thirds of assessed sites face moderate to high climate risk, pushing operators to factor resilience into Asia Pacific expansion plans.
stories.title_zh: 气候风险重塑亚太数据中心规划
stories.content:
Wed, 18th Nov 2026 (Today)
Cushman & Wakefield says 67% of assessed data centre sites in Asia Pacific face moderate to high climate risk, based on an analysis of more than 300 locations across 30 cities in 13 markets.

The report examines how hazards including flooding, extreme heat, drought, wind, fire, precipitation, hail and cold could affect data centre development and operations across the region. It says climate exposure is becoming a more immediate factor in decisions about where to build and expand capacity, alongside established considerations such as demand, connectivity and power access.

The analysis suggests the region's fastest-growing data centre markets are not always those with the lowest climate risk. Instead, operators are increasingly assessing whether a market can support reliable operations over time and whether surrounding infrastructure can accommodate further growth.

That shift reflects the practical effects of climate-related disruption on facilities that depend on stable power, effective cooling and business continuity. Flooding can affect site access and local infrastructure, while higher temperatures can increase cooling needs and strain electricity systems. Drought can also be a constraint where water is part of the cooling design.

Andrew Green, Head of Data Centre Group, Asia Pacific, Cushman & Wakefield, said: "Rather than slowing development, climate risk is reshaping how operators evaluate sites, plan infrastructure and prioritise investment across APAC. Operators are incorporating climate intelligence into site selection, engineering design and operational planning, recognising that resilience is critical to sustaining performance over the long term. As digital infrastructure requirements continue to grow, resilience will play a larger role in determining where and how capacity can be delivered."

### Location choices

The findings suggest location strategy is becoming more granular, with differences not only between countries but also between cities and submarkets. That means operators may need to assess climate exposure, infrastructure resilience and room for expansion together rather than as separate issues.

The report highlights several examples across Asia Pacific. It cites Johor as a case of rapid expansion that also raises infrastructure questions. Tokyo is presented as a mature market that continues to grow despite higher exposure to climate hazards. Mumbai is described as a market where demand remains strong in a higher-risk environment, while Sydney is highlighted for long-term planning and efforts to future-proof infrastructure assets.

Together, those comparisons reinforce a broader point: there is no single template for growth across the region. Markets differ in their mix of climate conditions, utility resilience, land supply and development constraints, so responses are likely to be local rather than uniform.

### Beyond the building

The analysis also argues that resilience now extends beyond the facility itself. Power networks, transmission systems and utility infrastructure are becoming more important to the investment case for data centres, especially as climate-related events place greater pressure on public infrastructure.

For operators, this shifts the focus from a narrow site assessment to a broader review of ecosystem readiness. Reliable electricity supply, grid stability and utility performance can shape whether a market remains attractive for large-scale expansion, particularly as artificial intelligence and denser computing workloads increase demands on power and cooling systems.

Matt Clifford, Head of Sustainability & ESG, Asia Pacific, Cushman & Wakefield, said: "Historical climate conditions are no longer sufficient inputs for long-term infrastructure planning. Climate intelligence should be integrated much earlier into investment, development and operational decisions to help organisations better understand future risks and improve resilience outcomes. Future-ready data centres will require planning assumptions that reflect tomorrow's climate realities, not yesterday's conditions."

The report was developed with Jupiter Intelligence, combining climate risk analytics with market data on the data centre sector. It covers more than 300 data centre locations, offering a regional view of how physical climate risks may influence future deployment and investment patterns.

Cushman & Wakefield says demand for digital infrastructure in Asia Pacific remains strong, driven by digitalisation, cloud adoption and artificial intelligence. But the study argues that demand alone will not determine which markets lead the next phase of development if operators also face rising exposure to climate-related disruption.

Pritesh Swamy, Head of Research & Consulting, Data Centre Group, Asia Pacific, Cushman & Wakefield, said: "Climate risk does not automatically determine investment outcomes. Many of APAC's fastest-growing data centre markets continue to attract investment despite differing risk profiles. Some markets benefit from lower climate risk, while others continue to thrive despite greater exposure because operators have invested in the infrastructure, planning and operational capabilities needed to manage those risks. The key for operators is to understand each market's unique risk profile and embed resilience into every stage of the data centre lifecycle."

stories.title: Can Malaysia build its own AI industry beyond data centres?
stories.summary: Summary Putrajaya is banking on private investments to support MD2030 while it focuses on digital infrastructure Tax incentives, affordable access to computing power and skills tr...

stories.title_zh: 马来西亚能否在数据中心之外建立自己的AI产业？
stories.content:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on November 9, 2026 - November 15, 2026

MALAYSIA’s ambition to become an artificial intelligence (AI) nation by 2030 will see the government focus its resources on building the digital infrastructure while counting on private investment to drive the country’s transition from a consumer of technology to a creator of its own.

Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo says Malaysia Digital 2030 (MD2030) — the latest phase of the digital transformation agenda — will not have a standalone budget. Instead, it will leverage existing government allocations, public-private partnerships and foreign and domestic private investment.

“We believe the strongest engine for achieving the scale and ambition of MD2030 will be private investment — both foreign direct investment (FDI) and domestic direct investment (DDI) — and public-private partnerships,” he tells The Edge in an email interview.

Public spending will focus on shared infrastructure, connectivity and digital platforms that lower costs for businesses developing new technologies.

“We want public investment to crowd in — not crowd out — private capital,” Gobind emphasises.

Incorporating the AI Action Plan 2026–2030, MD2030 seeks to raise the digital economy’s contribution to gross domestic product (GDP) to 30% by 2030, create 500,000 high-value digital jobs and spur the development of more Malaysian-made digital products, services and intellectual property (IP).

According to the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM), information and communications technology (ICT) and e-commerce contributed RM476.8 billion or 23.5% of GDP in 2025, up from RM451.5 billion or 23.4% a year earlier.

However, translating that growth into domestic technological capabilities remains a challenge, particularly as Malaysia aims to move beyond hosting data centres and cloud infrastructure for global tech giants.

While foreign capital has expanded the country’s digital infrastructure, questions remain over how much it actually builds local AI capability.

Gobind notes that the government evaluates investments based on the economic value they generate, including tech transfer, opportunities for local suppliers and local IP development. “We are interested not simply in the size of an investment but in its economic value-add. Does it create high-value jobs? Develop Malaysian talent? Transfer technology and knowledge? Deepen local supply chains? Generate intellectual property? And strengthen the ability of Malaysian companies to compete globally?”

He stresses that the government does not regard FDI and DDI as competing sources of capital, saying both are needed to develop the domestic technology industry. Initiatives such as the Government-Linked Enterprises Activation and Reform Programme (GEAR-uP) are examples of how Malaysian capital can be mobilised towards strategic and high-value sectors, he says.

However, SNS Network Technology Bhd (KL:SNS) co-founder and managing director Ko Yun Hung observes that Malaysian businesses remain largely at the adoption stage while foreign companies account for much of the investment in AI infrastructure.

“At this time, most of it is still foreign. Local companies are more in the adoption phase; investing in AI infrastructure is not common yet,” he tells The Edge.

Ko believes domestic investment is more likely to grow as businesses become more comfortable with AI and identify commercial use cases. For instance, a company that initially subscribes to AI services to automate administrative work or analyse sales data may eventually find it worthwhile to invest in its own computing infrastructure as usage increases.

To accelerate this transition, Ko suggests policy incentives such as accelerated capital allowances for technology purchases and double tax deductions for AI-related workforce training. It may be more effective to introduce incentives and programmes to motivate adoption and usage than providing direct grants to every business, he says.

For most Malaysian businesses, the immediate hurdle is not developing sophisticated AI products but figuring out how to integrate the technology to streamline and improve their existing operations.

Ko notes that companies of various sizes are generally receptive to AI, though many remain uncertain about where to begin due to fragmented or poorly organised internal data.

While generative AI tools such as ChatGPT have made the technology more accessible, businesses are increasingly exploring customised applications that can perform specific tasks, such as agentic AI. Such systems can be configured to carry out more complex tasks with varying degrees of autonomy, such as managing a company’s human resources department’s leave applications and flag potential staffing shortages before managers make their decisions.

Yet, few local companies have progressed towards developing their own AI applications, much less products that can be sold commercially, Ko says. “Maybe not yet. In terms of moving from ChatGPT to something more like agentic AI, we are seeing that, but still not to the extent of developing their own applications.”

Cost is a key barrier, particularly for smaller companies that are unable to justify purchasing expensive graphics processing units (GPUs) before knowing whether their AI projects will deliver the intended results.

To address this, SNS launched its AI Factory last year, offering GPU-as-a-Servic (GPUaaS) to businesses seeking computing capacity for developing, testing or deploying AI applications without having to purchase the hardware themselves. Starting with 64 GPUs, the facility allows businesses to test and deploy applications without heavy capital expenditure.

Expanding access to such capabilities is central to MD2030’s ambition of developing more Malaysian “AI Builders” — individuals and businesses capable of creating applications, AI agents and commercially viable products and services, according to Gobind.

“We want more Malaysians who do not simply know how to use AI tools but who can build with AI — people who can develop applications, AI agents, products and services, solve real problems using AI and ultimately turn those capabilities into new businesses and solutions.”

The government plans to encourage industry-led training, intensive boot camps, apprenticeships and other non-traditional learning pathways, alongside university and technical education.

Gobind also acknowledges that retaining these talents requires creating sufficiently attractive opportunities in Malaysia, particularly for engineers, researchers and entrepreneurs who might otherwise pursue careers overseas.

For small and medium enterprises (SMEs), the emphasis is expected to shift from basic digitalisation, such as e-commerce and digital payments, towards using AI to improve productivity and eventually develop their own solutions.

Ko believes Malaysian SMEs can make that transition by 2030, but warns that the relatively short timeframe will require businesses and policymakers to move quickly. “I am confident that SMEs will be able to become builders. My only worry is the time. When you talk about the AI world, the competition and progress are at a very fast pace.”

Beyond investment and talent, Malaysia must consider how much control it needs over the technologies underpinning its AI economy, particularly when much of the global ecosystem depends on foreign-developed chips, cloud platforms and software.

Gobind says Malaysia should remain open to international technologies and partnerships while developing domestic capabilities in areas where it can compete. “The government should not prescribe where Malaysian companies must compete. The market will ultimately determine where Malaysia can build a competitive advantage.

“At the same time, there may be strategic areas where considerations of national interest, resilience and technological sovereignty require the government to provide greater direction or support.”

Farlina Said, director of the Cyber and Technology Policy programme at the Institute of Strategic and International Studies (ISIS) Malaysia, points out that technological sovereignty does not necessarily require countries to develop every component of their technology infrastructure domestically.

“Where one would view end-to-end indigenous production as true sovereignty, others may have to consider diversification and clear responsibilities,” she tells The Edge.

Malaysia nevertheless needs its own computing capabilities, she argues, as such infrastructure is critical to national security, economic development and the ability to respond to emerging technological risks, even if it remains difficult to determine how much domestic computing capacity Malaysia will need while the AI landscape is evolving.

In the meantime, the country should diversify its infrastructure, build locally relevant AI models and strengthen technical expertise to reduce vulnerabilities arising from dependence on foreign technologies.

She also calls attention to regulatory gaps involving the ownership and safety of AI training data, accountability when government agencies deploy AI and the responsibilities associated with autonomous AI systems.

Malaysia’s existing laws address areas such as personal data protection, cybersecurity and online safety, but Farlina says regulation alone will not be sufficient without the technical expertise to scrutinise increasingly sophisticated AI systems. “Much needed is to build the capability that pierces the black box, whether it is through internal technical knowledge or information sharing.”

With less than four years to 2030, execution across ministries will determine MD2030’s outcome.

“Malaysia has developed strong policies and blueprints over the years. The challenge has often been translating those ambitions into coordinated execution across government and the wider ecosystem,” Gobind admits.

MyDIGITAL Corporation will oversee programme management and monitor implementation while reporting directly to the National Digital Economy and Fourth Industrial Revolution Council, chaired by the prime minister.

“Ultimately, accountability must mean more than reporting whether a programme is on schedule. We need to know whether it is delivering the intended outcome — and, if it is not, what needs to change,” the minister says.

Farlina advises evaluating headline targets, including the digital economy’s 30% contribution to GDP and the creation of 500,000 high-value digital jobs, alongside broader socioeconomic outcomes, noting that employment targets may be harder to assess as AI itself disrupts existing jobs.

“I think Malaysia needs to see that the AI Nation serves national interests and we must find ways to illustrate whether it is on track or deviating from socioeconomic goals,” she says.

Ko agrees that investment metrics alone are insufficient to determine whether Malaysia has successfully developed a domestic AI industry. “I think the measurement should not just be about how much foreign or domestic investment we attract. A stronger measure is how much our SMEs are being enabled,” he says. “Because of the uniqueness of each business, they may develop something using AI tools for their own operations and later realise that what they have developed can also be offered as a service and sold to others.”

stories.title: BNM sees strong data centre investment momentum until 2030 despite US chip restrictions
stories.summary: Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, maintains that data center investment flows into the country will remain robust through 2030 despite the uncertainty introduced by fresh US restrictions on chip exports to Chinese-affiliated operators. The assessment suggests Malaysian policymakers view the nation's neutral positioning and diverse investor base as insulating factors against geopolitical-driven project cancellations.
stories.why_it_matters: BNM's confidence reflects a calculated bet that Malaysia's multi-source investment pipeline—encompassing Middle Eastern, American, and domestic capital—can absorb any contraction in Chinese-backed developments. However, the central bank's timeline extends beyond the current policy cycle, exposing its forecast to potential escalation in US extraterritorial enforcement that could capture non-Chinese entities with indirect Chinese customer relationships.

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 18): Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) expects Malaysia’s data centre investment momentum to remain strong until at least 2030, even as fresh US chip export restrictions raise uncertainties over the sector’s growth prospects.

BNM governor Datuk Seri Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said it was too early to assess the impact of the US restrictions but pointed to Malaysia’s diversified base of data centre investors and sustained global demand for artificial intelligence (AI).

Of the 120 data centre companies in Malaysia, only 17 are Chinese companies while the rest are from countries including the US, Australia and Canada, as well as Malaysia, according to the governor.

“Based on our estimates of the ongoing and planned projects, the data centre investment momentum is expected to remain strong at least until 2030,” Abdul Rasheed said at a press conference announcing Malaysia’s third-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) figures on Wednesday.

“While there may be some reaction to these developments, we believe that the underlying demand is still strong,” he said.

Abdul Rasheed also pointed to the longer-term economic benefits of data centre investments beyond the construction phase, including the growth of information and communications technology (ICT) services exports and the creation of domestic economic linkages.

The US earlier this week announced new export controls requiring licences for shipments of certain advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, in an effort to prevent the diversion of sensitive American technology to China.

The new rules, scheduled to take effect on Nov 19, also tighten restrictions on overseas data centre operators providing significant computing capacity to companies headquartered in China and other jurisdictions of concern.

“This is an example of the geoeconomic risks that we are facing, not just us, but everyone else globally as well. As far as Malaysia is concerned, as Miti (Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry) has also said, we will continue to uphold rules-based trade, we are open for business, and our strategy is to serve everyone,” Abdul Rasheed said.

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 18): SCA Solutions Bhd said on Wednesday (Nov 18) that its operations remain on track and have no exposure to the latest US restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips.

Specialising in heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) as well as fire safety systems, the company derives 30% of its revenue from serving data centre clients.

“One thing I want to highlight is that the data centres we serve are mainly US-headquartered clients,” managing director Tan Cheng Eng told reporters at the prospectus launch.

“So we are not worried, because they \[data centre client\] have already approved the jobs and the works are already progressing,” Tan noted.

As of Oct, the company had an unbilled order book totalling RM46.7 million that will continue to provide revenue up to 2027.

Tan was responding to questions regarding the new US restrictions announced on Nov 16, which aim to prevent entities in China and other designated countries from remotely accessing advanced American AI chips through data centres in countries including Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The measures also introduce licensing requirements for imports of certain advanced AI chips, although companies headquartered in the US or whose ultimate parent companies are based there are exempt.

Tan further noted that the company's client base is not focused mainly on data centres but well diversified across various sectors, including residential, hospitals, educational institutions and semiconductor plants.

Asked about overseas expansion plans, SCA Solutions is looking to grow in Singapore and Indonesia, especially in serving the solutions for the water treatment segment, leveraging its existing client base and long-term relationships in both markets.

The water treatment segment contributes about 9% of the business while both regional markets contribute less than 1% of its most recent years’ revenue. However, Tan did not disclose specific growth targets.

For the financial year ended June 30, 2026, the group posted a net profit of RM7.95 million on revenue of RM51.33 million.

At the same time, SCA Solutions held cash and short-term deposits of RM15.95 million against RM7.56 million in bank borrowings.

SCA Solutions’ initial public offering (IPO) will raise RM47.85 million, of which RM31.92 million is for the company. The remaining RM15.93 million will accrue to the selling shareholders — Tan and executive director Liong Chian Leek.

stories.content:
The country’s stock benchmark falls near 16-month lows as ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s fall from grace signals heightened Sino-US tensions

\[SHANGHAI\] Equities in China and Hong Kong fell as investors continued to offload Chinese artificial intelligence hardware exporters and AI hyperscalers, amid signs of hardening US tech curbs against China ahead of a meeting between leaders Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump.

China’s stock benchmark was near 16-month lows as former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s fall from grace following Republicans’ defeat in the US midterm election foreshadowed an escalation in Sino-US tensions.

“The downfall of Jensen Huang could have consequences far beyond the AI sector, as tighter financing threatens the investment boom and political tensions reshape US-China relations,” Louis-Vincent Gave, founding partner of Gavekal Research, said in a note.

Both China’s blue-chip index CSI300 and the Shanghai Composite Index were down roughly 0.4 per cent by the midday break, flirting with the lowest level since mid-2025.

The Trump administration plans to press ahead with efforts to block imports of Chinese data centre equipment despite pushback from US technology companies.

Reuters reported in August that the Federal Communications Commission was seeking to ban US imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers over national security concerns.

And in a sign the US is tightening exports of advanced chips to China, Nvidia said the company would not rehire co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, and that its outlook assumes no data centre chip sales to China.

Huang had supported keeping sales open to China.

Chinese optical parts makers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink, which are heavily reliant on the US market, extended declines. They are down more than 70 per cent from their peaks.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Tech index lost 1.5 per cent, dragged lower by AI model developer MiniMax, as well as tech giants Alibaba and Tencent, whose businesses rely on advanced computing power.

However, China’s Star Chip Index rose 0.5 per cent and an index of China’s semiconductor industry gained, on bets that homegrown AI chipmakers will benefit from tighter US chip restrictions.

In other signs of geopolitical tensions, Trump met the leaders of key regional allies India, Japan and Australia in the Philippines on Tuesday, ahead of a much-anticipated trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen.

The Quad expressed “grave concerns” about “economic coercion” in a statement, without naming China.

Meanwhile, US Democratic Senator Tammy Baldwin on Tuesday introduced legislation to revoke China’s normal trade status and favourable tariff treatment.

In China, gold stocks tumbled nearly 5 per cent on higher expectations of US rate hikes, while defence stocks also fell sharply. REUTERS

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 18): Telekom Malaysia Bhd (KL:TM) could unlock additional earnings opportunities beyond 2030 from its RM2.7 billion undersea cable project, as growing artificial intelligence (AI) data centre investments in Sarawak drive demand for high-capacity connectivity, according to Kenanga Research.

The project, known as Sambungan Kabel Dasar Laut Madani (Salam), involves a 5,500km submarine cable connecting Peninsular Malaysia, Sarawak and Sabah. It will provide additional capacity as TM's existing undersea cable, Sistem Kabel Rakyat 1Malaysia (SKR1M), is already operating at about 85% capacity.

Kenanga in a note on Wednesday said AI data centres require substantial bandwidth, low-latency connectivity and reliable network infrastructure to support data transmission across Malaysia and international markets.

Salam's landing stations in Kuching and Bintulu (Samalaju) are strategically located near Sarawak's emerging data centre hubs, positioning TM to capture demand from upcoming developments.

Beyond providing bandwidth, TM could also act as an interconnection partner, linking data centres to internet exchange points, submarine cable systems and global connectivity networks. This would create opportunities to offer additional services such as indefeasible right of use (IRU), hot standby bandwidth allocation and managed wavelength services.

The project will run alongside SKR1M, which connects Peninsular Malaysia and Sabah and Sarawak. TM secured the SKR1M project, which is funded through the Universal Service Provision (USP) Fund, in December 2014 through a public-private partnership with the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC), with the cable commencing commercial operations in 2017.

For SKR1M, TM partnered TIME dotCom Bhd (KL:TIMECOM) under a 20-year construction and maintenance agreement, with an estimated ownership split of 83.6% and 16.4%, respectively. The arrangement was based on cost reimbursement without a profit-sharing mechanism.

By comparison, Salam is about 1.4 times longer and 3.8 times more expensive than SKR1M, with 10 landing stations compared with six previously.

Kenanga said Salam would further strengthen TM's international network, which spans more than 400,000km across 39 submarine cable systems.

The MCMC has designated TM as the universal service provider for Salam, which will be funded through the USP Fund. Construction is scheduled to begin in December 2026, with completion targeted in stages by the first quarter of 2030.

While the project is expected to contribute little to earnings during construction and its initial operational phase, Kenanga believes it could become a more meaningful earnings contributor beyond 2030 as demand for regional and international connectivity increases.

The research house estimated Salam's potential commercial value at RM523 million, equivalent to 13.6 sen per TM share, based on revenue from selling spare cable capacity.

Its valuation assumes that 90% of the RM2.7 billion allocation will be used for construction, with revenue from commercialising available capacity gradually reaching RM150 million annually by 2034.

Kenanga identified the pace of data centre development in Sabah and Sarawak as a key factor determining the project's earnings potential. Every RM50 million change in steady-state annual revenue could translate into a six to seven sen change in its estimated value per TM share.

However, the potential value has not been incorporated into Kenanga's current valuation pending greater clarity on the project's commercial terms.

The research house maintained its 'outperform' call on TM with an unchanged target price of RM9.11.

stories.content:
South-east Asia has a plan to share clean power. Can its data centres wait?

\[MANILA\] South-east Asia’s bid to become a hub for artificial intelligence is colliding with an awkward reality: Its power grids still run largely on coal and imported gas.

That tension took centre stage in Manila earlier this week, when all 11 Asean member states signed an enhanced memorandum of understanding (MOU) to build an integrated regional electricity network called the Asean Power Grid (APG).

The pact, which entered into force after the signing on Sunday (Nov 15), could determine whether the region’s booming data centre sector accelerates the green transition or locks in decades of fossil-fuel demand.

Designed to anchor cross-border interconnections, multilateral power trade and financing for overland lines and subsea cables, the agreement lands just as the COP31 conference in Turkey presses governments around the world to speed up clean electrification.

For South-east Asia, the immediate test is turning an influx of electricity-hungry digital infrastructure into fresh investments in renewable generation, storage and transmission.

Nowhere is that friction sharper than in the Philippines, which has just concluded its Asean chairmanship for 2026.

Manila is aggressively courting data centre operators as a pillar of its digital economy, yet its fragmented Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao grids remain plagued by transmission bottlenecks and recurring supply alerts.

More than nine in 10 Philippine business leaders say the country is overly reliant on fossil-fuel imports, the highest share among 18 economies surveyed by the Global Renewables Alliance (GRA), E3G and the We Mean Business Coalition.

## A regional answer to national bottlenecks

By pooling complementary energy resources across borders, the APG seeks to strengthen supply security and smooth the adoption of intermittent renewables.

For the Philippines, deeper regional links could eventually provide a vital buffer when domestic generation is tight.

“The enhanced MOU brings our commitment to partnership, innovation and resilience into practical focus,” said the country’s Secretary of Energy Sharon Garin, who stressed the value of attracting private and multilateral capital.

The pact complements the APG Financing Initiative, which brings together the regional bloc, the Asian Development Bank and the World Bank Group to mobilise funding for grid projects.

Under a high-renewables scenario, Asean estimates that it will require US$764 billion in generation and transmission investment through to 2045.

Global tech demand is adding urgency to that timeline. Electricity consumption by data centres rose 17 per cent worldwide in 2025, while demand from AI-focused facilities surged 50 per cent, according to the International Energy Agency.

Data centres accounted for roughly 40 per cent of corporate renewable power-purchase agreements (PPAs) signed globally last year.

In South-east Asia, however, procuring clean power is often easier on paper than in practice.

While the Philippines boasts retail competition, an open access regime, a green energy option programme and a liberalised wholesale market, developers and corporate buyers still contend with permitting delays, wheeling charges and congested transmission lines.

GRA’s Asia-Pacific regional lead Rexor Amancio said that grid investment must catch up with generation capacity so that transmission corridors are built in renewable-rich zones before connection queues stall new projects.

“Navigating the Philippines’ power market does not have to mean getting trapped in grid bottlenecks, but it does require closing the gap between commercial ambition and system infrastructure,” he added.

## Data centres as anchor customers

Clean-energy advocates argue that hyperscalers – the tech giants behind the world’s largest cloud and AI networks – should act as anchor customers for new solar, wind and geothermal projects, rather than simply buying up existing green supply.

Long-term corporate offtake deals can shore up the bankability of clean-energy and battery storage assets. Pairing generation with on-site batteries allows developers to serve immediate industrial demand, while flexible dispatch eases the strain on bottlenecked networks.

Hyperscalers have a direct commercial stake in funding grid upgrades upfront, not only to secure green electricity, but also to shield server farms from extreme weather, said Robert Cooke, GRA’s grids and electrification advocacy lead.

“Policymakers can mobilise data centres as a force for renewables,” he added.

Regulators are also under pressure to close accounting loopholes that let companies claim a “100 per cent renewable” status on paper by purchasing cheap annual green certificates, even while their servers hum through the night on coal-fired power.

Under frameworks such as the International Renewable Energy Agency’s COP31 green data centre programme, corporate buyers are being pressed to prove their electricity is newly built, locally sourced and matched hour-for-hour with consumption.

Amancio warned that if data centres “plug into a thermal-heavy grid and merely buy standard annual certificates or consume existing clean energy, they risk displacing green power from other users and driving up fossil gas at the margins, ultimately increasing power prices for everyone”.

Without faster grid connections, developers are already turning to dirtier workarounds.

BloombergNEF has reported that data centre builders frustrated by multi-year connection queues are increasingly installing dedicated onsite gas turbines – a stopgap that can be even more carbon-intensive than drawing power from a conventional grid.

stories.title: Govt targets minimum 30% local content for new data centres, says deputy minister
stories.summary: The government has set a minimum 30% local content target for new data centre projects approved under the Data Centre Task Force (DCTF), aiming to increase the participation of local companies in the development of the industry.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: 副部长称政府为新数据中心设定最低30%本地含量目标
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 18): The government has set a minimum 30% local content target for new data centre projects approved under the Data Centre Task Force (DCTF), aiming to increase the participation of local companies in the development of the industry.

Deputy Digital Minister Datuk Wilson Ugak Kumbong said the requirement covers engineering, maintenance, and network services, as well as technology provision.

He said the Malaysian Investment Development Authority monitors compliance with the relevant conditions through implementation reports submitted by companies every six months.

“At the same time, data centre operators are encouraged to implement local supplier development programmes to strengthen the capabilities of the domestic industry and promote technology transfer,” he said during the oral question-and-answer session in the Dewan Rakyat on Wednesday.

He was replying to a supplementary question from Datuk Seri Dr Wee Jeck Seng (Barisan Nasional-Tanjung Piai) about efforts to ensure that data centre growth also generates spillover benefits, such as talent development and business opportunities, for adjacent areas, including Pontian and Tanjung Piai.

Meanwhile, in response to Wee’s original question about the actual economic value generated versus the value of investments announced, Wilson Ugak said the data centre industry is capital-intensive and requires substantial initial investment.

He said a large portion of the equipment is imported, while capital expenditure is realised in stages throughout the project development period.

Thus, he said the announced investment value cannot be directly equated with actual total expenditure, job creation, or the value added to the local economy over a given period.

As of October 2026, 117 data centre projects have been approved in Malaysia, while approved investments for the data centre and cloud computing segment in the first half of this year totalled RM95.8 billion, he said.

Wilson Ugak said that under the DCTF, co-chaired by the Ministry of Digital and the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, 27 projects with an estimated investment value of RM225.97 billion had been approved as of October this year.

“In terms of employment, based on the outlook up to the second quarter of 2026, projects under the DCTF are expected to generate 4,053 job opportunities, including 3,523 high-skilled positions in the fields of electrical and mechanical engineering, networking and cybersecurity, as well as data centre operations and maintenance,” he said.

He said that although the number of direct jobs is lower than in sectors such as manufacturing, the data centre industry offers more specialised and highly skilled roles, while also creating indirect employment in the construction, engineering, and support services sectors.

He cited a Bank Negara Malaysia report for the third quarter of 2025, which indicates that entry-level positions in the industry offer salaries ranging from approximately RM3,000 to RM7,000 per month, while senior-level positions range from RM10,000 to RM30,000 per month.

“This salary level is higher than the monthly median salary for Malaysians, which stands at RM2,793 in 2024,” he said.

As for tax revenue, Wilson Ugak said direct contributions from corporate income tax are expected to increase gradually following the expiration of investment incentives currently enjoyed by some data centre projects.

However, he said the development and operation of data centres also contribute to government revenue through sales and service taxes, local authority assessment taxes, and revenue related to the consumption and supply of utilities.

He said the government has focused on human capital development through strategic collaborations with data centre operators, industry players, and training institutions to expand opportunities for industrial training, knowledge transfer, and professional certification.

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 18): CGS International sees new US artificial intelligence (AI) chip controls as a speed bump, not a structural derailment, for data centre (DC) spending in Asean, albeit with potential delays.

Malaysia and Thailand face greater exposure risks, but US hyperscaler relationships and contracted demand should cushion near-term earnings, it said.

The research house said Malaysia faces the greatest sentiment risk in the region, although AI DCs represent less than 10% of the installed capacity of about 1.3GW to which its covered companies are exposed.

“Malaysia’s energy, water and undersea cable capacities remain the key draws for DC investments,” CGS International said in a note on Wednesday, adding that these are likely to support demand growth over the next three to five years.

Of the 8.4GW of DC electricity supply agreements signed with Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA) as at June 2026, about 30% is linked to US-headquartered companies, while the bulk of the remainder is contracted by Singapore- and Malaysia-headquartered entities.

However, the firm cautioned that disclosures on the ultimate end-users are less clear, and it does not discount some indirect exposure to Chinese demand.

The trigger is the US Bureau of Industry and Security’s new export controls, effective Nov 19, 2026, which introduce destination-based licensing for advanced chips and servers supplied to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.

The new US rules create two licensing requirements. The first is a destination-based licence for exports, re-exports or in-country transfers of advanced chips and servers to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia (from which US-headquartered companies and subsidiaries of US-headquartered parents are exempt, subject to reporting obligations).

The second requirement is a global end-use licence for chips and servers used to provide computing capacity above 12 million aggregate total processing performance (TPP) to designated entities.

Existing data centres providing such services have 90 days to obtain the necessary authorisation.

They also add global end-use controls on computing access exceeding 12 million aggregate TPP for designated entities, including Chinese companies.

CGS International said the conditional exclusion for qualifying US-parented companies should favour US hyperscalers, while China-facing AI projects and independent graphics processing unit (GPU)-cloud operators face higher execution risks.

It expects the near-term impact on Asean to be felt mainly through slower AI-related capex and foreign direct investment into 2027, “as investors await licensing clarity”, with limited downside to Asean gross domestic product growth.

stories.title_zh: 模块化power conversion提升AI data center部署能力
stories.content:
Modular power conversion is transforming AI data centres by shifting the focus from the AC (Alternating Current) versus DC (Direct Current) power debate. This new approach emphasises how quickly capacity can be brought online, maintained through failures, and expanded without redesigning facilities.Higher-voltage DC architectures, such as 800 VDC, are gaining attention for AI compute due to their ability to reduce current and conversion stages. Modularity helps manage trade-offs inherent in any power architecture, especially when centralising conversion for efficiency and reliability.Operators are expected to adopt a mix of AC and DC approaches, with hybrid designs becoming common to suit varied workloads. Modular power systems, built and tested in factory environments, reduce onsite labour and logistical complexity, leading to faster and more predictable deployment.
### Enhanced Resilience and Scalability

Modular power conversion enhances resilience by enabling redundancy at the module level. This design reduces fault domains and allows maintenance without interrupting workloads, which is crucial for expensive AI training runs and inference services.The approach also addresses uncertainty in future power needs, allowing capacity to grow incrementally with demand. This prevents over-building and optimises capital use, simplifying planning with repeatable building blocks. A systems-level view is essential, integrating power, thermal, and operational components into a scalable whole.

stories.title: Malaysia's Q3 growth beats forecasts as tech boom lifts economy
stories.summary: The country has attracted billions of dollars in data centre investments

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: 马来西亚Q3增长超预期，科技繁荣提振经济
stories.content:
The country has attracted billions of dollars in data centre investments

\[KUALA LUMPUR\] Malaysia’s economy grew 5.5 per cent in the third quarter, surpassing expectations as a result of sustained household spending and robust tech exports driven by the AI boom, government and central bank data showed on Wednesday (Nov 18).

Economists polled by Reuters and advance estimates released by the government had forecast annual gross domestic product to expand 5.3 per cent in the July to September period, slowing from 6 per cent in the second quarter.

Growth in the third quarter was underpinned by strong domestic demand as well as higher levels of investment and tourism activity, according to data from Bank Negara Malaysia and the Statistics Department.

While some moderation in private consumption was observed during the quarter, this was attributed mostly to base effects, BNM Governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said.

“Looking ahead, the Malaysian economy is well positioned to build on this momentum in 2027, supported by strong fundamentals and positive outcomes from our structural reform,” he said.

The government raised its 2026 growth projections in October, and now expects the economy to expand close to the upper end of a 4.8 per cent to 5.3 per cent forecast range.

It expects growth of between 4.2 per cent and 5.2 per cent in 2027.

### Data centre investments to remain strong

Malaysia has benefited from the global artificial intelligence boom, which has boosted exports of its semiconductors and other tech goods.

Exports rose 5.7 per cent from a year earlier, with shipments of electrical and electronic goods jumping 66.9 per cent, according to Friday’s data.

The country has also attracted billions of dollars in data centre investments, though analysts have warned that growth in the sector could slow following US curbs aimed at restricting China’s access to advanced AI chips.

Abdul Ghaffour said it was too early to assess the impact of the latest restrictions but said data centre investments in Malaysia were expected to remain strong until 2030, based on estimates of ongoing and planned projects.

Out of 120 data centre companies, just 13 per cent were Chinese firms, with the rest from the US, Australia, Canada and Malaysia, he said.

“It’s very well diversified... while there may be some reaction to (the latest curbs), we believe underlying demand is still strong,” he said.

BNM kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged for the eighth straight meeting earlier this month. Economists, however, expect the central bank to raise the rate in the first quarter of 2027, amid resilient growth and growing price pressures.

Inflation was expected to edge higher to a range of 1.5 per cent to 2.5 per cent in 2026 and 1.8 per cent to 2.8 per cent in 2027, but it would remain contained, Abdul Ghaffour said.

He declined to comment on whether the central bank would hike rates, saying BNM would continue to monitor to see if price pressures were building widely and consistently.

“If it happens, we have the space, we can be decisive in terms of our actions,” he said. REUTERS

stories.title: Assessing liquid cooling readiness for AI racks in colocation halls
stories.summary: Data center operators must assess liquid cooling readiness for specific racks and rows before deploying AI infrastructure. This includes confirming rack power, coolant requirements, and heat rejection capabilities to ensure operational reliability. The assessment helps prevent capacity limits and service disruptions for existing tenants.
stories.title_zh: 评估colocation机房中AI机架的liquid cooling就绪度
stories.content:
Data center operators must assess liquid cooling readiness at the rack and row level in existing colocation halls, not the entire facility, before deploying high-density AI infrastructure. This assessment ensures that new loads can be supported without affecting neighbouring tenants, according to Mark Deguara, Technology Innovation Leader at Schneider Electric.Operators should confirm rack power, liquid-to-air heat split, coolant requirements, row electrical capacity, floor loading, and installation access. These checks are crucial before committing to density figures or delivery dates for new deployments. Heat rejection must be validated at local summer design conditions and during planned maintenance periods.
### Key Infrastructure Dependencies

Coolant distribution units (CDUs), heat dissipation units (HDUs), rear door heat exchangers, and facility water systems introduce dependencies. These components can limit usable high-density capacity within a colocation hall. The wider cooling plant also impacts the overall readiness.Retrofit economics depend on shared infrastructure and the tenant rollout plan. Operators should compare targeted row conversion, dedicated hybrid zones, or modular expansion options. This comparison should use the same load, service conditions, outage requirements, and future reuse assumptions.Commissioning and tenant agreements should reflect the capacity that was actually tested. Acceptance criteria must cover maintenance states, leak and loss-of-flow response, coolant management, and responsibility boundaries. This ensures clear operational guidelines for both the operator and the tenant.

stories.summary_zh: 中国国家主席习近平在与美国当选总统Donald Trump预期会谈前的讲话中警告称，protectionism正在升级，直接提及限制中国公司通过overseas data centers和third-country routing获取芯片的新美国规则。这一时机将北京的外交立场与BIS interim final rule对中国AI发展的直接商业影响联系起来。

stories.content:
New US rules released this week target Chinese companies’ use of overseas data centres and access to chips through third countries

XI JINPING urged Asia-Pacific economies to deepen cooperation as he warned against rising unilateralism and protectionism, setting out a defence of free trade as China hosts global leaders for high-stakes talks on trade and technology.

“Global growth lacks momentum, and unilateralism and protectionism are rampant,” the Chinese president told the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday (Nov 18). He called for closer technology partnerships and efforts to keep global supply chains stable and open.

“China has stood up unilateralism and protectionism and remained committed to true multilateralism,” Xi said, vowing to cut tariffs, expand market access and foster a more stable environment for foreign investments.

China will play host to a week of diplomacy and dealmaking as the Apec event get underway. Xi has already wrapped up several bilateral meetings, including talks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during which both countries agreed to further tariff relief on agricultural and steel exports.

Xi is also expected to meet with his US counterpart, Donald Trump, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, before sitting down with them together for unprecedented talks between the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers.

The Xi-Trump summit coincides with an escalating US push to restrict China’s access to the computing power needed to develop advanced AI.

New US rules released this week target Chinese companies’ use of overseas data centres and access to chips through third countries, drawing a threat of retaliation from Beijing just days before Xi meets Trump to shore up their fragile trade truce.

In addition to Xi, the leaders of 11 other Apec economies — including Australia, Chile, Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico and Vietnam — are also attending the CEO Summit that runs on Nov 17-18, state media Xinhua News Agency reported.

Even as Xi showcases China’s tech prowess in Shenzhen, the world’s second-biggest economy is flashing numerous warning signs.

Official figures released on Monday showed a slowdown across the board, underscoring the sluggish domestic demand that’s prompted complaints from China’s major trading partners. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: MHI and SAKURA internet to form strategic alliance to build Japan's sovereign AI infrastructure
stories.summary: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and SAKURA Internet will establish a strategic alliance to develop domestically controlled AI and cloud computing infrastructure in Japan, explicitly targeting reduction of dependence on foreign-operated platforms. The partnership combines MHI's industrial engineering capabilities with SAKURA's internet infrastructure expertise to create what both parties describe as sovereign AI infrastructure.
stories.why_it_matters: Japan's sovereign AI push reflects a broader G7 trend toward technological decoupling that will fragment cloud market architecture and create parallel supply chains for sensitive workloads. Domestic infrastructure providers gain policy tailwinds and procurement preferences, while US and Chinese hyperscalers face incremental exclusion from government and critical infrastructure contracts in one of Asia's largest data center markets.

stories.why_zh: 日本的sovereign AI推动反映了G7更广泛的技术脱钩趋势，这将分裂cloud market架构，并为敏感工作负载创建parallel supply chains。国内infrastructure提供商获得政策顺风和采购偏好，而美国和中国的hyperscalers在亚洲最大的data center市场之一面临来自政府和critical infrastructure合同的渐进式排斥。
stories.content:
Japanese engineering and manufacturing major Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd. (MHI), and digital infrastructure provider SAKURA internet Inc. have announced the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to form a strategic alliance to explore collaboration to strengthen Japan’s domestic digital infrastructure for sovereign AI and cloud. The initiative includes developing AI modular data centers.

The strategic alliance comes amidst burgeoning demand for AI and cloud infrastructure, as well as growing concerns over data sovereignty, given how much of the AI processing in Japan runs on cloud platforms operated overseas.

MHI and Sakura aim to collaborate to build a secure, high-performance, Japan-based digital infrastructure foundation for the sovereign AI and sovereign cloud era and offering vertically integrated services. They also plan to highly efficient AI data centers quickly for AI infrastructure, and explore reference architectures and modular construction methods for mechanical and electrical equipment.

“As AI becomes national infrastructure, that infrastructure has to be resilient in both how it is built and how it is operated. With SAKURA internet, we want to give Japan a sovereign AI foundation that is secure, available when it matters, and fast enough to keep pace with demand. This is part of MHI ITO\*2 initiative: combining our strengths with the right partner to deliver value to far more customers,” said Masayuki Suematsu, Executive Vice President and Chief Strategy Officer, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd.

“With the rapid spread of AI, digital infrastructure such as cloud and data centers has become essential to society and industry. In this collaboration, we will combine MHI’s technology and expertise in social infrastructure with our own experience building and operating cloud and data centers. Together, we aim to create new options for the domestic digital infrastructure that the sovereign AI and sovereign cloud era requires,” said Kunihiro Tanaka, Founder, Chief Executive Officer, and President, SAKURA internet Inc.

MHI is strengthening its data center business, which integrates cooling, power, control and high-security technologies. SAKURA internet operates data centers in Tokyo, Osaka and Hokkaido and has an extensive track record in building and operating data centers and cloud services. Looking ahead, the two companies aim to take the products and solutions established through this collaboration to global markets, including Asia and Oceania.

stories.title: US AI chip curbs could bring more data centre jobs to Malaysian contractors — Maybank IB
stories.summary: New US restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips could benefit Malaysian construction companies by creating more opportunities for them to secure data centre contracts, according to Maybank Investment Bank Research.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: 美国AI芯片限制可能为马来西亚承包商带来更多数据中心工作机会——Maybank IB
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 18): New US restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips could benefit Malaysian construction companies by creating more opportunities for them to secure data centre contracts, according to Maybank Investment Bank Research.

The research house said the restrictions pose limited risks to local contractors, as their major US-headquartered data centre clients are exempt from new import licensing requirements.

In a note, Maybank IB said US-headquartered clients account for 100% of the outstanding data centre order books of Sunway Construction Group Bhd (KL:SUNCON) and IJM Corp Bhd (KL:IJM) and 95% of Gamuda Bhd's (KL:GAMUDA).

As such, it sees little risk of existing data centre construction contracts being cancelled.

The US announced new restrictions on Nov 16 aimed at preventing entities in China and other designated countries from remotely accessing advanced American AI chips through data centres in countries including Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The measures also introduce licensing requirements for imports of certain advanced AI chips, although companies headquartered in the US or whose ultimate parent companies are based there are exempt.

Maybank IB said the restrictions could also give American-owned data centre operators greater room to expand in Malaysia if Chinese-owned operators face difficulties pursuing new projects.

It noted that American and Chinese operators compete for land, electricity and water while Chinese-owned operators rarely award data centre construction contracts to Malaysian contractors.

"If the new restrictions are successful in preventing Chinese-owned data centre operators from expanding in Malaysia, American owned ones will have more scope to expand," it said.

This could also allow Malaysian contractors serving American-owned data centre operators, including Gamuda, IJM and Sunway Construction, to secure more contracts, the research house added.

As for Binastra Corp Bhd (KL:BNASTRA), Maybank IB said its main data centre client, Malaysia-headquartered EXSIM, intends to comply with the new licensing requirements by shifting towards US-headquartered tenants.

Against this backdrop, Maybank IB maintained its positive outlook on the Malaysian construction sector, with Sunway Construction remaining its top pick and a target price of RM9.62.

It also upgraded IJM to 'buy' from 'hold', while maintaining its target price of RM2.83.

The research house retained its 'buy' calls on Gamuda and Binastra, with unchanged target prices of RM5.47 and RM3.40 respectively.

Looking ahead, Maybank IB said investors should watch for potential catalysts in upcoming quarterly results, including stronger earnings from Gamuda as construction projects progress, further data centre contract wins for Binastra and developments involving IJM’s proposed construction business listing.

stories.title: Blackstone joint venture buys AWS data center campuses for $5 billion
stories.summary: Blackstone's Digital Infrastructure Trust purchased a 75 percent stake in two joint ventures holding AWS data center campuses for roughly $5 billion, with AWS committing to a 12-year leaseback arrangement. This sale-leaseback structure represents Amazon's first such deal for its cloud infrastructure assets, providing Blackstone with long-term contracted revenue while freeing AWS capital for other investments.
stories.why_it_matters: The transaction signals deepening institutional investor appetite for hyperscale data center exposure and validates sale-leaseback as a viable capital recycling tool for cloud operators. AWS competitors may face pressure to monetize their real estate portfolios similarly, while the 12-year lease term sets a benchmark for long-duration infrastructure pricing in an environment of rising interest rates and construction costs.

stories.content:
Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC) has completed a definitive agreement to acquire a 75 per cent majority interest in two joint ventures with Amazon Web Services (AWS). This transaction is valued at approximately $5 billion.AWS will retain a 25 per cent interest in the joint ventures and will lease back the facilities on a triple net basis for an initial term of 12 years. This arrangement means AWS will cover rent, real estate taxes, building insurance, and maintenance costs.The acquired properties consist of 13 newly constructed data halls with an aggregate capacity of 647 megawatts. One campus, comprising nine buildings, is located in northern Indiana within the greater Chicago data center market. The other campus, with four structures, is in Mississippi.An AWS spokesperson confirmed this is the first deal of its kind signed by the company. Prasad Kalyanaraman, VP of AWS Infrastructure, stated that partnering with Blackstone allows AWS to expand responsibly while prioritising communities.Alan Howard, principal analyst for Colocation and DC Building at Omdia, suggested that sale-leaseback transactions can be more economical. He noted that massive capital expenditure for AI buildout is pressuring hyperscaler financials, making such deals potentially more attractive. This transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026.The agreement includes a provision for either party to terminate the deal if it does not close by December 31, 2026. In such a scenario, the non-breaching party would be entitled to a termination fee of $150 million.

stories.title: China warns US of retaliation over new AI chip restrictions
stories.summary: China's foreign ministry and commerce ministry issued formal warnings of countermeasures against the United States following the release of new AI chip export restrictions, with officials stating the measures threaten to destabilize bilateral relations ahead of Xi Jinping's scheduled meeting with Donald Trump. Beijing characterized the restrictions as technological hegemony that violates international trade norms and harms Chinese enterprise interests.
stories.why_it_matters: The explicit retaliation threat creates immediate uncertainty for US semiconductor equipment makers and materials suppliers with China revenue exposure, while forcing multinational data center operators to accelerate geographic diversification of their supply chains. The timing before a leadership summit suggests Beijing seeks leverage to extract carve-outs or delay implementation, but failure to secure concessions would likely trigger targeted restrictions on US cloud services or rare earth materials.

stories.content:
The restrictions threaten to overshadow Xi’s meeting with Donald Trump this week

CHINA warned the US it would retaliate if Washington proceeds with curbs on remote access to advanced chips, while urging the Trump administration to resolve differences through dialogue.

The Ministry of Commerce in Beijing on Tuesday (Nov 17) expressed “strong dissatisfaction and firm opposition” after the US unveiled sweeping new restrictions on China’s access to high-end AI chips. Those curbs came days before President Xi Jinping is set to host his American counterpart for their third summit of the year.

“China hopes the US will work with us in the same direction and return to the right track of resolving differences through consultation and cooperation,” the ministry said in a statement. “If the US persists, China will take countermeasures to firmly safeguard its sovereignty, security and development interests.”

The measures run counter to understandings reached by the two countries’ leaders and threaten the stability of global semiconductor supply chains, the ministry added.

A fragile trade truce that brought down sky-high tariffs between the two superpowers last year is currently set to expire in January.

Rules released on Monday by the US Commerce Department seek to prevent Chinese companies from renting Nvidia semiconductors outside the US and obtaining processors through Singapore and several other countries.

They risk putting technology restrictions back at the centre of US-China tensions just as the leaders prepare to shore up their delicate detente.

The restrictions threaten to overshadow Xi’s meeting with Donald Trump this week on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen.

Officials from the world’s biggest economies are also expected to hold their first AI dialogue over safety issues, a discussion that may now be coloured by their disagreement over hardware access.

Beijing has been bracing for tougher US curbs since the downfall of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who had been the industry’s most prominent opponent of chip controls against China.

Huang resigned last week amid revelations about extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former executive at a Singapore-based company under scrutiny over suspected chip smuggling and whom the US suspects of being a Chinese spy.

As the tech rivalry with Beijing intensifies, Trump is seeking to deepen AI cooperation with India, Australia and Japan.

Leaders of the so-called Quad group held their first summit in two years in Manila on Tuesday, when Trump also promoted deals to reduce the nations’ reliance on “any single foreign supplier” for critical minerals, in a likely reference to China. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Azure Cobalt 200 VMs now generally available
stories.summary: Microsoft has announced the general availability of Azure Cobalt 200-based virtual machines (VMs) across 14 regions. These VMs offer up to 50 per cent better performance than Cobalt 100 for cloud-native, database, developer, and agentic AI workloads. Availability will expand to 23 regions by the end of 2026.
stories.title_zh: Azure Cobalt 200 VM正式发布
stories.content:
Microsoft has announced the general availability of Azure Cobalt 200-based virtual machines (VMs). These VMs are now available in 14 Azure regions and will expand to 23 regions by the end of 2026.Cobalt 200 VMs deliver up to 50 per cent better performance than Cobalt 100, according to Microsoft. They are designed for cloud-native, data-intensive, and agentic AI workloads.The company expects Cobalt 200 VMs to represent a significant share of new Azure Compute capacity starting in 2027. Customers like Amadeus, Databricks, InMobi, OpenAI, and Snowflake have reported improved performance and efficiency over Cobalt 100 VMs.This allows customers to achieve faster search results, more responsive database queries, and higher service utilisation with fewer cores. Cobalt 200 VMs include Microsoft Azure Boost for accelerated network and remote storage performance.
### Technical Specifications and Workload Optimisations

The Cobalt 200 system-on-chip (SoC) is built on TSMC’s advanced 3nm process technology. It features 132 Arm Neoverse V3 cores and a multi-chipset architecture.Microsoft has added two new VM families for Arm-based compute on Azure. These include High-memory Mpsv4 for large in-memory databases and Storage-optimized Lpsv5 for workloads needing fast local NVMe storage.Benchmarking for Cobalt 200 VMs showed up to 1.5 times increased performance for web serving and AI agent tool execution workloads. Java-based workloads saw up to 1.6 times higher performance, and database workloads up to 1.9 times over Cobalt 100.Microsoft products and services, including Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure DevOps, and Microsoft 365, run on Cobalt VMs. The company’s silicon engineers reported increased performance and efficiency for EDA workloads on Cobalt 200 VMs.Vadim Filanovsky, a Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI, stated that Cobalt 200 delivered higher throughput and lower latency for ChatGPT workloads. This enables serving more users with the same number of cores.Vinod Marur, SVP Engineering at Databricks, noted that Azure Databricks serverless compute on Cobalt starts faster and runs more efficiently. Murray Stokely, Distinguished Engineer at Snowflake, highlighted real performance and efficiency gains for their workloads with each Cobalt generation.Luc Choubert, VP Engineering at Amadeus, reported that Azure Cobalt 200 improved flight search throughput by over 30 per cent compared with Cobalt 100. Sudheer Bhat, Principal Engineer at InMobi, observed performance and efficiency improvements for their ad-serving workloads.
